descriptor: Matching set on pollutants: the substance once blended into U.S. gasoline to improve engine performance.
solution: Tetraethyl lead was added to gasoline to prevent engine knock until it was phased out in the United States. Lead is a persistent neurotoxic metal, so the correct match is lead. Mercury, copper, iron and radon were never fuel additives.
notes: FORM CHECK: this file (Form O, form code 4MBP, 2016) has page-for-page identical text to the 2016 US exam file in the uploads (66327176-2016_AP_Environmental_Science_Exam__Released_for_Teacher_Use.pdf); the document itself never states US or Intl, so it is not a different form. Treat as a duplicate of the US 2016 register; MCQ/FRQ entries here should be de-duplicated against it.

descriptor: Matching set on pollutants: the gas that forms when uranium in rock undergoes radioactive decay.
solution: Uranium decays through a series of daughter products, and one of them is radon, a colorless, odorless noble gas. It seeps up from rock and soil, so it is the gaseous decay product. The metals listed are solids and are not products of uranium decay in this sense.

descriptor: Matching set: the pollutant that ranks among the leading causes of lung cancer in the United States.
solution: Radon accumulates in poorly ventilated basements and ground-floor rooms, and its radioactive decay products lodge in lung tissue. After smoking it is a leading cause of lung cancer. Lead and mercury act mainly on the nervous system and kidneys, not as lung carcinogens.

descriptor: Matching set: the pollutant that endangers people who regularly eat large predatory ocean fish such as swordfish and tuna.
solution: Mercury is converted by microbes to methylmercury, which is fat-soluble and persistent, so it bioaccumulates in organisms and biomagnifies up marine food chains. Top predators such as swordfish and tuna carry the highest concentrations. The other listed substances do not biomagnify in this way.

descriptor: Map-location set: which lettered region stores vast methane hydrate deposits whose release would strongly intensify warming.
solution: Methane hydrates lie in Arctic permafrost and cold shallow seafloor sediments. As the Arctic warms they can destabilize and release methane, a potent greenhouse gas, creating a positive feedback. The correct point is the high-latitude northwestern marker, not the temperate or tropical ones.

descriptor: Map-location set: the region now warming fastest on average because of human-caused climate change.
solution: The Arctic is warming at more than twice the global average because loss of reflective ice and snow exposes darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight (ice-albedo feedback). The high-latitude marker is therefore correct. Low-latitude regions are warming more slowly.

descriptor: Map-location set: the area where damaging tornadoes are most frequent.
solution: Tornadoes form where cold, dry air from the north and west collides with warm, moist Gulf air over flat terrain, which is characteristic of the central United States (Tornado Alley). The marker placed over the U.S. interior is correct. The other markers lie in Africa, the Middle East or the Arctic, where this air-mass clash does not occur.

descriptor: Map-location set: the region where tropical forest fragmentation by people is causing major biodiversity loss.
solution: The marker in central Africa sits over the Congo Basin, a large tropical rain forest where logging, farming and road building split habitat into small patches. Small isolated patches support fewer species and raise extinction rates. The other markers are in a desert, the Middle East, North America and the Arctic.

descriptor: Map-location set: the region that has led the world in crude oil exports for roughly four decades.
solution: The Middle East, with Saudi Arabia as the dominant exporter, holds the largest concentration of conventional oil reserves and has been the top exporting region for decades. The marker on the Arabian Peninsula is therefore correct.

descriptor: Plate-boundary map set: which lettered area shows island arcs.
solution: Island arcs form where an oceanic plate subducts beneath another plate, and the sinking slab melts to feed a curved chain of volcanoes. The western Pacific marker lies on such a subduction margin. Mid-ocean ridges and continental collisions do not produce island arcs.

descriptor: Plate-boundary map set: the area with a rising mountain chain that is not volcanic, built by uplift.
solution: Where two continental plates collide, neither subducts easily and the crust is thrust upward into non-volcanic fold mountains. The India-Eurasia collision producing the Himalaya is the marked area. Subduction margins produce volcanic ranges instead.

descriptor: Plate-boundary map set: the area where new crust forms at a divergent boundary.
solution: At divergent boundaries plates move apart and magma rises to build new oceanic crust, as along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The marked point on the North Atlantic spreading boundary fits. The other marked areas are subduction or collision zones.

descriptor: Five climatographs are shown. Choose the climate with the greatest tree species diversity.
solution: Tropical rain forest has the highest tree diversity, and its climatograph shows high temperature all year and heavy precipitation in every month. Graph B is the only one with these steady warm, wet conditions. Cold, dry or strongly seasonal climates support fewer tree species.

descriptor: Using the same five climatographs, pick the climate expected to have dry scrub with frequent fires.
solution: Chaparral and similar scrub occur where summers are hot and dry and rain falls in mild winters. Graph C shows warm temperatures year-round with almost no summer rain, which dries vegetation and makes fire common. The other graphs show wetter or colder patterns.

descriptor: A table gives total fertility, infant mortality and life expectancy for five countries. Identify the one most likely to be shrinking.
solution: Replacement-level fertility is about 2.1 births per woman, and a country well below it will eventually shrink, ignoring migration. Country C has a fertility rate of 1.8 and a long life expectancy, so its population is most likely declining. Countries D and E are at or above replacement, and A and B are far above it.

descriptor: Same country table: which country most likely offers women limited educational opportunities.
solution: Low female education is strongly linked to high fertility, high infant mortality and short life expectancy. Country A has the highest fertility rate (6.5), the highest infant mortality and the lowest life expectancy, matching that profile. The other countries show indicators typical of better education and health care.

descriptor: Choose the process that the Sun's radiation does NOT power.
solution: Solar energy drives photosynthesis, ocean currents, hurricanes and cloud formation through heating and evaporation. Plate tectonics is powered by heat from Earth's interior, so it is the exception.

descriptor: Explain why phytoplankton concentrate in the top few hundred feet of water bodies.
solution: Phytoplankton photosynthesize, so they must live in the photic zone where light is available. Light is absorbed and scattered as it passes through water, so it fades with depth. Their abundance there is about light, not predator avoidance or being bottom-dwellers.

descriptor: Which pair of exhaust pollutants do catalytic converters reduce?
solution: A catalytic converter uses platinum-group metal catalysts to oxidize carbon monoxide to CO₂ and unburned hydrocarbons to CO₂ and water, and it also reduces nitrogen oxides. Carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons is the pair. Converters do not remove CO₂, lead or mercury, and they are not designed for particulates.

descriptor: Which statement correctly describes how a fuel cell vehicle works?
solution: A hydrogen fuel cell combines hydrogen with oxygen in an electrochemical reaction that produces electricity, water and heat, and the electricity runs the motor. That is the statement about using hydrogen to generate electricity. The other options describe hybrids, biofuels, solar cells or steam turbines.

descriptor: Choose the graph showing soil organic matter falling over time under intensive farming without manure or fertilizer.
solution: Without inputs of residues or manure, decomposition and crop removal deplete organic matter. The loss is fastest at first and slows as the remaining matter becomes more resistant, giving a curve that falls steeply and then flattens. Graph C shows this decreasing, leveling curve; the other graphs show increases or the wrong variables.

descriptor: On a soil texture triangle, read the sand, silt and clay percentages at point T.
solution: Reading the triangle at T gives 60% sand, 30% silt and 10% clay, which sums to 100%. Each corner of the triangle is 100% of one component, so each point is read along three sets of gridlines.
notes: Point T sits between gridlines on the triangle and the exact reading was confirmed only approximately; the keyed answer was accepted.

descriptor: Which marked soil composition would make the best landfill liner?
solution: A liner must be nearly impermeable so leachate cannot escape. Clay particles are the smallest and pack tightly, so soils with the highest clay percentage have the lowest permeability. Point W has by far the most clay, whereas the other points contain much more sand and silt.

descriptor: A diagram shows warm air lying above cold air beneath a limited mixing depth over a city. Name the phenomenon.
solution: A thermal inversion occurs when a layer of warm air sits above cooler air near the ground. The cooler air cannot rise past the warm layer, so pollutants are trapped in a shallow mixing depth and concentrations build up during pollution episodes.

descriptor: Select the true statement about the Ogallala Aquifer.
solution: The Ogallala Aquifer lies beneath the High Plains of the central United States. It supplies irrigation for large amounts of cropland, and withdrawals have exceeded natural recharge for decades, so water levels are falling. The other options place it on the wrong continents or describe wrong problems.

descriptor: Predict how climate change will shift red pine, which now lives only in cool northern areas.
solution: As average temperatures rise, species adapted to cool climates tend to move toward higher latitudes or elevations. Red pine's suitable range should therefore move northward into Canada. It would not expand into warmer regions to the south.

descriptor: Choose the sequence that shows a positive feedback loop in the warming Arctic.
solution: Melting ice exposes darker ocean water that absorbs more sunlight, so surface water warms, and the warmer water melts more ice. Each change reinforces the one before it, which is the definition of positive feedback. The other sequences reverse a step and create a damping or inconsistent loop.

descriptor: A student predicts shade from a planned desert solar plant will raise creosote bush mortality. What baseline data should be collected before construction?
solution: The hypothesis ties plant mortality to shade, so the relevant baseline variable is how much sunlight the plants receive now at the site. Measuring direct sunlight in kWh per square meter over a year provides a before-and-after comparison. Global CO₂, noise, erosion or precipitation do not address shading.

descriptor: A graph shows biomass of five tree species after clear-cutting. When is species richness highest?
solution: Species richness is the number of species present. At 100 years all five plotted species show biomass above zero, since sweet gum has not yet disappeared and hickory and beech have arrived. At 50 years hickory and beech have not yet arrived, and by 150 years sweet gum is gone.

descriptor: From the same succession graph, which species does best in full sunlight?
solution: Sweet gum rises quickly in the open, sunny conditions just after clear-cutting and then declines as the canopy closes and shades it. That boom-and-bust pattern marks a sun-loving pioneer species. The oaks, hickory, beech and dogwood increase later in shade.

descriptor: Explain why many deserts lie near 30° north and south latitude.
solution: Warm air rises at the equator, cools and loses its moisture as heavy tropical rain, then spreads poleward and sinks near 30° latitude. Sinking air warms and becomes dry, producing the low humidity and desert belts. The other options reverse the air movement or invoke winds and rain shadows that are not the global cause.

descriptor: Identify which item is NOT household hazardous waste.
solution: Household hazardous waste includes batteries, pesticides, motor oil and oil-based paint because they are toxic, flammable or corrosive. Food scraps are ordinary organic waste that can be composted or landfilled, so they are the exception.

descriptor: Why do hybrid electric vehicles use less fossil fuel per mile than conventional cars?
solution: Hybrids use regenerative braking, which converts the vehicle's kinetic energy into electricity to recharge the battery instead of wasting it as heat. The battery then assists the motor, so the engine burns less fuel. Hybrids still burn gasoline, and standard hybrids are not plugged in or solar powered.

descriptor: Why do small isolated islands suffer higher extinction rates than larger, less isolated ones?
solution: Island biogeography theory predicts that small islands have fewer resources and niches, so their populations are small and more likely to disappear. Isolation also reduces immigration that could rescue populations. Fewer resources is therefore the correct reason, while the other options describe increases in species.

descriptor: On a logistic population curve, what does the dashed horizontal line labeled K represent?
solution: In an S-shaped growth curve the population levels off where births balance deaths, at the maximum number the environment can sustain. That limit is the carrying capacity, symbolized K. Biotic potential and intrinsic growth rate refer to the unconstrained growth rate instead.

descriptor: Choose the diagram that correctly depicts the nitrogen cycle.
solution: Nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N₂ into ammonium (NH₄⁺); nitrification then converts ammonium to nitrite and nitrate, which plants can take up; and denitrification returns N₂ to the air. Diagram A shows these linked steps in the right order, while the others show impossible conversions.

descriptor: A graph shows glyphosate use and the number of glyphosate-resistant weed species both rising from 1990 to 2010. Pick the best explanation.
solution: Repeated spraying of the same herbicide kills susceptible weeds and leaves those with resistance genes to survive and reproduce. This natural selection explains why more resistant species appear as use increases. The graph shows rising use, so the options claiming use fell are wrong, and it provides no yield or profit data.

descriptor: Identify a concern linked to the growing share of genetically modified crops.
solution: When farmers plant large areas with a few uniform GM varieties, the genetic diversity of crops shrinks, leaving them more vulnerable to new pests or diseases. The other statements are not accepted concerns or are factually wrong about GM crops.

descriptor: How might herbicides in farm runoff contribute to the decline of amphibians?
solution: Some agricultural chemicals interfere with hormone signaling and act as endocrine disruptors, which can cause developmental and reproductive abnormalities in amphibians, whose permeable skin readily absorbs pollutants. The other options give mechanisms that do not describe herbicide effects.

descriptor: A graph shows U.S. electricity from coal, natural gas, nuclear and renewables from 1950 to 2010. Which inference is best supported?
solution: The graph shows coal generation peaking and then falling around 2008 while natural gas and renewable generation rise, so growth of those sources is a reasonable explanation. The graph says nothing about coal shortages, nuclear construction costs or federal wind laws, so those causal claims are unsupported.

descriptor: Select the age structure diagram for a population with negative growth.
solution: A shrinking population has few young people and a larger share of older age groups, so its diagram narrows at the base. Diagram D is narrow at the bottom and wider above, indicating births below the level needed to replace the population. Wide-base pyramids indicate fast growth.

descriptor: A table gives temperature, shading, turbidity, dissolved solids, pH and hardness for five stream sites. Which site likely lies just downstream of a construction site?
solution: Construction exposes bare soil, and runoff carries sediment into the stream, raising turbidity and total dissolved solids sharply. Site C has turbidity of 100 NTU and 2,000 mg/L solids, far above the others. Site E differs mainly in pH, which suggests acid input rather than soil disturbance.

descriptor: Corn needs a given land area per kcal and beef needs 20 times more. Choose the setup for land needed to produce 10,000 kcal of beef.
solution: Beef takes 20 times as much land per calorie as corn, so each kcal of beef needs the land that would produce 20 kcal of corn. At 1 ha per 1,000 kcal of corn, the chain is 1 ha/1,000 kcal corn × 20 kcal corn/kcal beef × 10,000 kcal beef = 200 ha. Setup B has that structure and cancels units properly.

descriptor: Which is an advantage of generating electricity with nuclear power?
solution: Fission releases energy without combustion, so the reaction emits no carbon dioxide during operation. The other options are false: nuclear power produces radioactive waste, uses finite uranium, is expensive to build, and releases waste heat that can cause thermal pollution.

descriptor: Which soil constituent is most likely to neutralize acid rain?
solution: Limestone is calcium carbonate, a base that reacts with hydrogen ions and buffers acidity. Soils rich in limestone resist acidification from acid deposition. Granite, sand, radon and humus lack this neutralizing capacity.

descriptor: World growth is projected to slow from about 1% to 0.5% by 2050. Besides access to birth control, which is another likely cause?
solution: As more women in developing nations enter the paid workforce, the opportunity cost of childbearing rises and women tend to have fewer children, lowering fertility. The other choices would raise growth or are not expected to lower it.

descriptor: How does an El Niño event reduce brown pelican numbers in southern California?
solution: During El Niño, ocean surface waters warm and upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water weakens. The fish pelicans eat move to cooler water farther from nesting sites, so adults cannot feed chicks and the population falls. The other mechanisms are not accepted explanations.

descriptor: Why do the open oceans hold the largest share of Earth's biomass?
solution: Open-ocean net primary productivity per unit area is low because nutrients are scarce, but the oceans cover most of the planet. The huge area supports enormous numbers of phytoplankton, so total production is large. The option claiming high productivity is wrong.

descriptor: A smog-day graph shows NO peaking in the morning and then falling. Which statement explains the pattern?
solution: Nitric oxide is released by rush-hour vehicle engines, producing the early morning peak. In sunlight it is quickly oxidized to NO₂ and consumed in smog reactions, so its concentration falls. NO is a primary pollutant and participates in smog formation.

descriptor: If technology lowered hydrocarbon emissions on that smoggy day, what is the most likely result?
solution: Photochemical smog forms when sunlight drives reactions between hydrocarbons (VOCs) and nitrogen oxides, generating ozone and aldehydes. Cutting hydrocarbons removes reactants, so less ozone forms. The other options predict higher ozone or changes unrelated to the reaction.

descriptor: A table compares five reclaimed coal mine sites after ten years. Pick the site with the most successful forest reclamation.
solution: Successful forest reclamation means trees dominate. Site 5 has the highest tree cover (65%) and the fastest seedling growth (20 cm/yr), while its grass cover is lowest, so grass is not competing heavily with the seedlings. The other sites have less tree cover and slower growth.

descriptor: A housing development replaces small farms. What is its greatest impact on the local water supply?
solution: Roofs, driveways and roads are impervious, so less rain soaks into the ground, and groundwater recharge decreases. Runoff increases rather than decreases, so the other options reverse the expected changes.

descriptor: What will stormwater runoff from the new development likely do to a nearby creek?
solution: Construction and impervious surfaces speed runoff that carries sediment and suspended solids into the creek. High turbidity smothers fish eggs and bottom habitat and reduces light. The other options name unrelated pollutants or diseases that do not follow from stormwater.

descriptor: What step could homeowners in the development take to protect creek water quality?
solution: Rain barrels capture roof runoff, reducing the volume and speed of stormwater entering the creek and lowering the pollutant load. Applying fertilizer before storms, dumping pet waste into storm drains and using persistent pesticides all worsen pollution, and channelizing a creek increases erosion.

descriptor: Beak sizes differ between two nearby Galápagos islands for the same species. Which hypothesis best explains the difference?
solution: Beak size is genetic and the islands are close, so the difference likely reflects natural selection by different food types, such as seed size and hardness, on each island. Birds on Santa Cruz show consistently larger beaks than those on Daphne, which fits food-driven selection.

descriptor: Replacing 5-gallon-per-minute showerheads with 2-gallon-per-minute ones, a family of five showers 8 minutes each per day. How much water is saved in 30 days?
solution: Savings per minute are 5 − 2 = 3 gal. Time per day is 5 people × 8 min = 40 min, so the daily saving is 3 gal/min × 40 min = 120 gal. Over 30 days, 120 gal/day × 30 days = 3,600 gal.

descriptor: What does hydraulic fracturing do to boreholes in rock?
solution: In fracking, high-pressure fluid containing sand and chemicals is pumped into a well to create cracks in tight rock. The sand holds the cracks open so trapped oil and natural gas can flow to the well. It does not pulverize rock or reopen mines.

descriptor: How do demographics change as a country begins moving from a preindustrial to an industrial state?
solution: In the early transition, improved food supply and sanitation lower death rates while birth rates stay high, so the population grows rapidly. Birth rates fall only later. The other options either have population decreasing or death rates rising.

descriptor: Which item is NOT a negative externality?
solution: A negative externality is an unpaid cost imposed on others, such as illness near a factory, airport noise, refinery air pollution or crop damage from exhaust. Bees pollinating neighboring vegetables is a benefit to others, so it is a positive externality.

descriptor: A graph shows land-use percentages in four watersheds. Which statement is most likely true?
solution: Watershed II is dominated by residential and commercial land, which has many impervious surfaces, so runoff reaches streams quickly and flow swings sharply with rainfall. Watershed III has less developed land, and watershed I is mostly forest so it should not have severe algal blooms or low oxygen.

descriptor: A farmer plans 40% tree crop and 60% vegetables on her land. Which equation gives total income?
solution: Total income equals the income per hectare for each crop times the hectares devoted to it. Trees occupy 0.4 of the total hectares and vegetables 0.6, so the equation is (income per ha trees × total ha × 0.4) + (income per ha vegetables × total ha × 0.6). Option D assigns the fractions to the correct crops and includes total area.

descriptor: What does surface ocean circulation most directly accomplish?
solution: Surface currents driven by winds carry warm water from the tropics toward the poles and cold water toward the equator, redistributing heat around the planet. Overturn of lakes, the jet stream and ocean acidification are not direct results of surface circulation.

descriptor: Use a decay curve of moles versus time to estimate the half-life.
solution: Half-life is the time for the amount to fall to half its starting value. The curve starts at 0.20 mol and reaches 0.10 mol after roughly 7 seconds, so the half-life is closest to 7 seconds.

descriptor: What most likely caused the recent blue-green algae blooms in Lake Erie?
solution: Phosphorus in fertilizer and manure running off farmland fertilizes the lake, causing eutrophication and cyanobacterial blooms. Cooler temperatures would reduce blooms, and the other options are not major nutrient sources.

descriptor: Native alpine plants have declined while invasive grasses have increased. Which investigative question is most appropriate?
solution: Air pollution deposits nitrogen onto soils, and nitrogen-rich soil favors fast-growing invasive grasses over native plants adapted to poor soil. That makes the nitrate question a plausible, testable cause. The other questions rest on unrelated or illogical mechanisms.

descriptor: An experiment tests lethal doses of ammonium sulfate on mung bean germination. Which statements about the design are true?
solution: The independent variable is the concentration of ammonium sulfate that the researcher changes, and the dependent variable is the number of seeds that fail to germinate. A proper control group has seeds with no ammonium sulfate, so statement I, which says there are no seeds, is false.

descriptor: What is a major limitation of photovoltaic cells?
solution: Photovoltaic output depends on sunlight, so it drops on cloudy days and is zero at night. They produce little CO₂, have no moving parts and can connect to the grid, so the other options are not limitations.

descriptor: Besides fertilizers, vehicle exhaust and industrial air pollution, what is another major human source of nitrogen pollution?
solution: Sewage contains nitrogen compounds from human waste, and discharge into surface waters adds nitrogen that causes eutrophication. The other options release other pollutants, such as refrigerants or hydrocarbons, not nitrogen.

descriptor: A car averaging 30 mpg and another at 20 mpg each drive 60,000 miles; 20 lb CO₂ per gallon. How many fewer pounds does the 30 mpg car emit?
solution: Gallons used: 60,000 ÷ 30 = 2,000 gal versus 60,000 ÷ 20 = 3,000 gal, a difference of 1,000 gal. At 20 lb CO₂ per gallon, 1,000 gal × 20 lb/gal = 20,000 lb fewer.

descriptor: Which policy would most likely push fertility above replacement level?
solution: Giving public housing priority to larger families lowers the cost of raising more children, which encourages higher fertility. The other measures promote small families or discourage larger ones, which lowers fertility.

descriptor: Which statement is true of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990?
solution: The 1990 amendments created a cap-and-trade program for sulfur dioxide that let power plants buy and sell emission allowances to reduce acid rain. They did not regulate CO₂ or lower fuel economy standards.

descriptor: A table of water-quality data from five creek sites is given. Which site is most likely immediately downstream of a dairy farm?
solution: Manure and fertilizer runoff raises nitrate, phosphorus and fecal coliform counts, and decomposing waste consumes oxygen. Site C has the highest nitrate (40 mg/L), phosphorus (1.00 mg/L) and coliform (500 colonies/100 mL), the lowest dissolved oxygen (1.5 ppm) and the lowest macroinvertebrate diversity.

descriptor: Which route most likely moves mercury into the food web?
solution: Burning coal emits mercury to the air, which falls to land and water by deposition. Aquatic microbes convert it to methylmercury, which plankton absorb and which then biomagnifies through fish. The other pathways are unlikely or incorrect.

descriptor: Two soil samples are rich in carbon and nitrogen and dark; four are low. What is the likely explanation?
solution: The A horizon (topsoil) contains abundant decomposing organic matter, which is dark and holds carbon and nitrogen. The B horizon is mainly mineral and low in organic material. Samples from A horizons would therefore be dark and rich in C and N.

descriptor: What kills trout and other fish during eutrophication?
solution: Excess nutrients cause algal blooms, and when the algae die, bacterial decomposition consumes dissolved oxygen. Fish then suffocate from lack of oxygen. Eutrophication does not primarily cause toxic pH, mercury or salt.

descriptor: Why do utility bills for coal-fired electricity understate the true cost?
solution: Coal power imposes external costs, such as respiratory disease from air pollution, that are paid by society, not reflected in consumers' bills. The bills do include distribution and marketing costs. The other options incorrectly say that environmental damage is included.

descriptor: Which is an example of a carbon sink?
solution: A sink stores more carbon than it releases. Organic matter that settles on the deep ocean floor is buried for long periods, removing carbon from circulation. Forest clearing, fuel combustion and decomposition release carbon, and a lawn's nutrient uptake does not store it long term.

descriptor: A map shows population doubling times by country. Which statement is best supported?
solution: A shorter doubling time means faster growth. India appears in a shorter doubling-time class (41-80 years) than China and Australia (81-200 years), so its growth rate is higher. The map provides no data on population size, density or arable land.

descriptor: Which problem is fracking most likely to cause?
solution: Fracking fluids and released gas or brine can migrate into aquifers or leak from wells, contaminating groundwater. It is not associated with ozone depletion, eutrophication, denitrification or desertification.

descriptor: Rangers suspect trampling killed alpine plants near a trail. Which comparison best tests the hypothesis?
solution: A hypothesis about trampling is tested by comparing plant survival where hikers stay on the trail with survival where hikers leave it, since trampling is the variable. Counting hikers or comparing their characteristics does not measure plant response.

descriptor: What reproductive approach does K-selection use?
solution: K-selected species live near carrying capacity and invest heavily in few offspring with considerable parental care, which raises each offspring's chance of survival. Producing many offspring with little care describes r-selection.

descriptor: 60% of 2 kg of daily waste per person is compostable. How much is compostable per week?
solution: Daily compostable waste is 0.60 × 2 kg = 1.2 kg. Over seven days, 1.2 kg/day × 7 days = 8.4 kg.

descriptor: Which is NOT a likely result of Arctic warming?
solution: Floating sea ice is already displacing its own mass of water, so melting it does not raise sea level and does not create new farmland. The other scenarios describe actual consequences, such as permafrost methane release and habitat shifts.

descriptor: Net primary productivity differs among three forest biomes. Which factors explain the variation?
solution: Productivity is controlled by temperature and precipitation: warm, wet tropical forests grow fastest, and cold northern forests grow slowest. Longitude is not a climate factor that drives productivity.

descriptor: Which would most likely lower ground-level ozone in a city?
solution: Ground-level ozone forms when sunlight drives reactions between NOₓ and VOCs, so reducing nitrogen oxide emissions slows ozone formation. Sunny days, inversions and added VOCs increase ozone, and CFCs are not a major factor.

descriptor: On a latitude diagram, which latitude has 24 hours of daylight on December 21?
solution: On December 21 the Southern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so the Antarctic Circle (66.5° S) and everything south of it receives continuous daylight. Marked latitude E is on the Antarctic Circle.

descriptor: Which describes bioaccumulation?
solution: Bioaccumulation is the buildup of a substance in an organism when it absorbs the substance faster than it can eliminate it. It is not nutrient uptake, transfer between generations or restricted to oceans.

descriptor: Which health effect is most closely linked to atmospheric particulates?
solution: Fine particles irritate and enter the lungs, triggering asthma and other respiratory disease. Cataracts and melanoma are linked to UV exposure, and diabetes and obesity are not primarily caused by particulates.

descriptor: A timber company plans to harvest oaks and hickories 50 years after clear-cutting. Which fact best supports claims that it is unrealistic?
solution: After clear-cutting, fast-growing pioneer species colonize first, and slow-growing late-successional oaks and hickories take many decades or longer to return to harvestable size. A 50-year harvest of large oaks is therefore unrealistic.

descriptor: Pick the best example of the tragedy of the commons.
solution: The tragedy of the commons occurs when many users degrade a shared resource because each acts in self-interest. Oil-rig pollution in the shared Gulf is the choice that best matches. Overharvest of privately owned lakes is not commons since owners control access, and the other options are unrelated.
notes: Keyed answer A reads awkwardly (the option stresses pollution concentration rather than open-access overuse); it is the best match among the options, since option E concerns privately owned lakes.

descriptor: Volcanoes emit CO₂ and sulfate-forming particulates. How do carbon dioxide and stratospheric aerosols affect climate?
solution: CO₂ absorbs infrared radiation and contributes to warming. Stratospheric aerosols reflect incoming sunlight and cause cooling. They do not both warm, and CO₂ does not convert into aerosols.

descriptor: Which pairing correctly links a human health effect to a source of fine particulate matter?
solution: PM2.5 from coal power plants and other combustion penetrates deep into lungs and is linked to respiratory disease. The other pairings link effects to causes that do not produce fine particles.

descriptor: Why does human-produced water vapor not contribute significantly to global warming?
solution: Water vapor is a greenhouse gas, but it condenses and falls as precipitation within days, so its concentration is set by temperature and does not accumulate. Added emissions leave quickly and have little long-term effect. It does absorb energy and does have warming effect.

descriptor: Why are infectious diseases expected to spread as climate changes?
solution: Warmer temperatures extend the range where insects such as mosquitoes and ticks can survive, exposing people in areas once too cold. The other statements are inaccurate or not the main reason.

descriptor: A school project tests whether more plant species in pasture benefits ranchers. Which supported hypothesis shows an economic benefit?
solution: Higher net primary productivity means more forage, which can support more livestock and increase income. Lower water infiltration, soil pH or bird diversity do not show a benefit.

descriptor: Graphs show irrigation water use and money earned for different crops. What do they best explain?
solution: The returns graph shows that vegetables and fruit give the highest income per liter of water, while livestock, pasture and grains give the lowest. The graphs do not support statements about prices, consumption or resource use of cattle.

descriptor: What global change is expected from higher atmospheric CO₂ over 50 years?
solution: Rising CO₂ is expected to cause significant biodiversity loss in the tropics as temperatures and rainfall shift faster than species can adapt. The other options describe the opposite of expected trends: more severe storms, more frequent heat waves, and earlier rather than delayed spring events.

descriptor: Graphs show regional meat consumption, meat production and projected population. Which statement is consistent?
solution: The consumption graph shows North Americans eat about 320 g of meat per day per person, the highest of any region. The other statements link per capita use to population trends that the graphs do not support.

descriptor: Which health effect is most associated with a thermal inversion?
solution: An inversion traps pollutants including fine particulates near the ground, which irritates the respiratory system. Skin cancer, mold, infant mortality and heart attacks are not directly caused by inversions.

descriptor: Which annual growth rate is paired with the correct doubling time?
solution: The rule of 70 gives doubling time = 70 ÷ growth rate (%). At 2% this is 35 years. The others do not match: 1% gives 70 years, 3.5% gives 20 years, 5% gives 14 years, and 7% gives 10 years.

descriptor: Newspaper article on white-nose syndrome killing little brown bats: why disease rarely causes extinction, threats to a tiny population, slow recovery, effects on other species, forest ecosystem services, and why human emerging diseases are increasing.
solution:
**(a) Why disease seldom drives a host to extinction.** Any one of: genetic variation in a wild population means some individuals resist infection and reproduce; pathogens and hosts co-evolve so the host evolves defenses; a pathogen that kills every host also destroys its own habitat; or early deaths lower population density so transmission slows. *(1 point: a valid explanation)*

**(b)(i) Two threats to a very small bat population.** Examples: difficulty finding mates when individuals are scarce and scattered; competition from similar species for roosts or insects; loss of genetic diversity (inbreeding, a population bottleneck, one disease able to affect all); less group protection or less shared warmth; greater vulnerability to a named disturbance such as drought or habitat loss. *(2 points: 1 for each described threat, first two only)*

**(b)(ii) Slow recovery.** Little brown bats have low fecundity (one or two pups a year), long generation times, late first reproduction and heavy parental care, so numbers rebuild slowly even if mortality stops. *(1 point: a correct aspect of bat biology with the link to slow recovery)*

**(c) Effects on other organisms of a bat decline.** Examples: insect prey increase, which can raise insect-borne disease and crop pests; plants that bats pollinate or whose seeds they disperse decline; predators of bats lose food; competitors with similar needs increase; a trophic cascade follows. *(2 points: 1 for each described effect, first two only)*

**(d) Two forest ecosystem services.** For each, name the service and the human benefit, for example: timber and fuel (materials), water filtration and flow regulation (clean water, flood control), soil protection (agriculture), carbon storage (slows climate change), habitat and biodiversity (food, medicine, recreation), or cultural and recreational value (tourism, education). *(2 points: 1 for each service paired with a benefit to people)*

**(e) Reason for more emerging human diseases.** Give a reason and explain it, for example: climate change lets pathogens and vectors survive in new areas; more global travel moves infected people and animals quickly; more contact with wildlife through habitat loss and the wildlife trade lets zoonotic diseases cross over; higher population density speeds transmission; low vaccination lowers herd immunity; antibiotic resistance creates new strains. *(2 points: 1 for a valid reason, 1 for a correct explanation of how it raises disease emergence)*
notes: Same Form O (4MBP) text as the US 2016 file; duplicate of the US entry. Article text and figure are not reproduced; solutions are written from the scoring criteria's ideas in original wording.

orig_ref: a32fb6ac-2016Intl-2, pdf p.43 (booklet p.4), scoring pp.49-50, FRQ2
descriptor: Iron and steel production data: calculate rock waste from ore to pig iron, pig iron from total reserves, reserves used for steel, and coal saved by recycling; then abandoned coal mine problems, a remedy, and why surface mining costs less.
solution:
**(a)(i) Rock waste per year.** Waste = ore in − pig iron out = 1.6 × 10⁹ t − 1.2 × 10⁹ t = 0.4 × 10⁹ t = **4 × 10⁸ tons** of rock waste per year. *(1 point: correct answer with work)*

**(a)(ii) Pig iron from all reserves.** Yield = 1.2 ÷ 1.6 = 0.75 t pig iron per t ore. (1.2 billion t pig iron ÷ 1.6 billion t ore) × 800 billion t ore = 0.75 × 800 = **600 billion tons** (6.0 × 10¹¹ t). *(2 points: 1 for a correct setup using the ratio, 1 for the answer)*

**(a)(iii) Reserves used for steel.** 0.95 × 800 billion t = **760 billion tons** of ore (7.6 × 10¹¹ t). *(1 point: correct answer with work)*

**(b) Coal conserved by recycling.** 0.7 t coal saved per t steel recycled × 80 million t steel = **56 million tons of coal per year** (5.6 × 10⁷ t). *(1 point: correct answer with work)*

**(c) Two problems at abandoned coal mines.** Examples: acid mine drainage and heavy-metal runoff degrading streams; subsidence and sinkholes from collapsed shafts; habitat loss that recovers slowly; erosion and dust from bare tailings; methane release; underground fires. *(2 points: 1 for each described problem, first two only)*

**(d) Mitigation of one problem.** Examples: treat acid drainage with limestone or hold it in retention ponds; plant vegetation or regrade land to control erosion; fill or fence shafts to stop subsidence and access; return tailings to the pit. *(1 point: a correct method matched to a problem named in (c))*

**(e) Why surface mining is cheaper.** Choose a reason and link it to cost: fewer workers are needed and wages are lower (labor cost); fewer severe accidents, deaths and black lung cases mean lower insurance, healthcare and legal costs (safety); no tunneling, ventilation or roof support is needed. *(2 points: 1 for a reason, 1 for a correct discussion of why it lowers the cost)*
notes: Same Form O (4MBP) text as the US 2016 file; duplicate of the US entry. Part (a)(ii) in the guideline refers to the result as tons of iron, but the quantity is pig iron; a reader should accept 600 billion tons either way.

orig_ref: a32fb6ac-2016Intl-2, pdf p.44 (booklet p.5), scoring pp.51-52, FRQ3
descriptor: Graph of U.S. municipal solid waste, total and per capita, 1960 to 2012: cause of per capita change, percent increase calculation, incineration and landfill drawbacks, landfill-gas electricity steps, tire piles, composting pros and cons.
solution:
**(a)(i) Cause of the change in per capita waste, 2000 to 2012.** Per capita generation fell slightly (from about 4.7 to about 4.4 lb per person per day). A valid cause: more reduction, reuse or recycling; lighter packaging (plastic instead of glass, thinner cans); less material in products; digital media replacing paper; or lower consumption during the recession. *(1 point: a plausible, explained cause other than composting)*

**(a)(ii) Percent increase in total MSW, 1980 to 2012.** Reading the graph, about 150 million tons in 1980 and about 250 million tons in 2012. Percent increase = (250 − 150) ÷ 150 × 100 = **≈ 67%** (accept 66–67%). *(1 point: correct answer with work)*

**(b)(i) Incineration disadvantage.** Emits air pollutants (CO₂, particulates, dioxins, NOₓ, SOₓ); leaves ash that needs safe disposal; costly to build and operate; may need extra fuel when waste is low in quality; neighbors object. *(1 point)*

**(b)(ii) Landfill disadvantage.** Can contaminate groundwater or soil through leachate; releases methane and CO₂; odors and vermin; uses land and destroys habitat; lowers nearby property values; explosion hazard from methane. *(1 point)*

**(c) Electricity from buried waste.** Step 1: collect the methane (landfill gas) produced by anaerobic decomposition through wells and pipes. Step 2: burn the gas to heat water or air, converting chemical energy to thermal energy and producing steam or hot gas. Step 3: the steam or hot gas spins a turbine connected to a generator, producing electricity. *(3 points: 1 for each step)*

**(d) Health problem from tire piles.** Standing water in tires breeds mosquitoes that carry disease, or tire fires release smoke and toxic chemicals that cause respiratory problems. *(1 point)*

**(e)(i) Composting advantage.** Produces soil amendment or fertilizer that can be used or sold; creates jobs; reduces odor and landfill fees. *(1 point)*

**(e)(ii) Composting disadvantage.** Piles can attract vermin, smell or catch fire; they release methane; nutrients can run off into water; it takes labor and time. *(1 point)*
notes: Same Form O (4MBP) text as the US 2016 file; duplicate of the US entry. Graph values (about 150 and 250 million tons) are read from the figure; per capita values are approximate.

orig_ref: a32fb6ac-2016Intl-2, pdf p.45 (booklet p.6), scoring pp.53-54, FRQ4
descriptor: Soil question: how two climate factors affect soil formation rate, biotic and abiotic parts of the A horizon, nitrate in groundwater from farming, acid deposition effects and remediation, and two ways climate change degrades soil.
solution:
**(a) Two climate factors and soil formation rate.** Temperature: warmth speeds weathering and decomposition and so speeds soil formation; cold slows biological activity (though freeze-thaw can break rock). Precipitation: moderate to high rainfall speeds chemical weathering and biological activity; very heavy rain can erode soil and slow accumulation; dry climates slow formation. Wind can deposit particles that add soil or blow it away. *(2 points: 1 for each described effect, first two only; naming a factor alone earns nothing)*

**(b) A horizon components.** Biotic: humus, microorganisms, fungi, earthworms, insects or roots. Abiotic: sand, silt, clay, water, air, minerals or nutrient compounds. *(2 points: 1 for a specific biotic component, 1 for an abiotic component)*

**(c)(i) Practice raising nitrate.** Heavy application of nitrogen fertilizer, or poorly sealed feedlots or manure lagoons. *(1 point)*
**(c)(ii) How.** Nitrate is highly soluble and not held by soil particles, so excess dissolves in water and percolates down to groundwater or flows into surface water that recharges aquifers. *(1 point: description linked to the practice)*

**(d)(i) Effect on plants.** Acidified soil can fall outside the plant's tolerance range; it leaches nutrient cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺) so they are unavailable; it frees aluminum that is toxic to roots; it reduces buffering capacity. *(1 point)*
**(d)(ii) Remediation.** Add crushed limestone or lime (calcium carbonate) to neutralize acidity. *(1 point)*

**(e) Two ways climate change degrades soil.** Examples: warmer, drier conditions cause desertification; higher evaporation of irrigation water causes salinization; heavy rainfall increases erosion and leaching; higher temperatures speed organic matter breakdown; sea level rise floods coastal soils with salt water. *(2 points: 1 for each described way)*
notes: Same Form O (4MBP) text as the US 2016 file; duplicate of the US entry.
